title: Time's Answer to Arjuna
subtitle: Vyasa consoles the grieving archer, and Parikshit is enthroned
story:
Arjuna, the great archer of the five Pandava brothers, had leaned on Krishna through everything. When word came that Krishna had left the world, and his elder brother Balarama with him, Arjuna went to Dwaraka alone.

Dwaraka, Krishna's city by the sea, was a city of the dead. Arjuna performed the last rites for the two brothers and for all the slain. Krishna's eight queens, Rukmini at their head, embraced their lord's body and entered the funeral fire; Revati, holding the body of Balarama, entered it too, and the fire, the old account says, was cool to her. Hearing this, Ugrasena and Vasudeva, Krishna's own father, with Devaki and Rohini, gave themselves to the flames. Arjuna performed their rites as well, and then made the whole city rise and leave — taking Vajra, the young prince of the Yadava line, and leading the thousands of Krishna's wives and all the people slowly away, with tenderness and care.

Behind them, the Sudharman palace and the Parijata tree, which Krishna had once brought down to earth, rose and returned to heaven. That same day the dark age of the world, the Kali age, began; and the ocean rose and covered all of Dwaraka except one small temple of the Yadava deity, which the sea has never washed away. There, they say, Krishna still abides, and whoever visits it is freed from his sins.

Arjuna halted the great company in the Panchanada country, a rich and fertile land. There the robbers of the region saw one lone warrior guarding so many widowed women and so much treasure, and their greed woke. They gathered the lawless Abhiras to them. "Here is Arjuna," they said, "rich and proud of slaying Bhishma and Drona and Karna. He does not know the courage of simple villagers. Up! Take your staves!" And they rushed at the people with cudgels and clods of earth.

"Go back, wretches," Arjuna called, "unless you wish to die." They paid him no heed; they seized the treasure and the women. Arjuna reached for Gandiva, his great heavenly bow — and it would not brace. The string stayed slack, however he strained. The words that called the superhuman weapons would not come back to him. He loosed arrows as best he could, and they only scratched the skin; even the shafts the fire-god Agni had given him were destroyed. He beat at the bandits with the horn of his bow, and they laughed. And before his eyes, the barbarians carried off the women of the Vrishni and Andhaka clans and went their way.

Then the greatest archer of the age broke down. "Alas, alas!" he wept. "I am deserted by my lord!" And in that instant Gandiva and the heavenly weapons, his chariot and his horses, perished before his eyes. "Resistless are the decrees of fate," he said, "which gave feebleness to me and victory to the base. These arms are mine; this fist is mine; I am Arjuna. But without him who stood beside me, all of it is hollow — and without him I am overcome by peasants."

He went on to Mathura and set the young prince Vajra on its throne. There, in a wood, he found the sage Vyasa and bowed at his feet. Vyasa looked at him a long while. "How is it, Arjuna," he asked, "that I see you shorn of your brightness? Have you been beaten by your inferiors in battle?"

Arjuna sighed and told him everything. "Krishna, who was our strength, our heroism, our very brightness, has left us," he said. "Without him we are as weak as straw. Gandiva, famed through three worlds, is foiled by the sticks of peasants; the household of Krishna is carried off by thieves with cudgels. It is not that my brightness is gone — it is a wonder that I live."

Vyasa's answer was gentle, and it was absolute. "Think no more of your disgrace, my son," he said. "Know that time bends all beings the same way: rivers, seas, mountains, gods, men, trees, insects — all are created by time and destroyed by time. Krishna came down to lift the burden of the earth, and that work is done. The kings are slain, the Vrishni race is destroyed; nothing was left for him to do, and so he has departed, his purpose fulfilled. Your defeat by miserable thieves was as much his work as your victories over Bhishma and Karna. It is only the play of the lord of all."

Then Vyasa told him a story. Long ago there was a sage named Ashtavakra, a brahman whose body was bent in eight places. For years he stood in water, meditating. When the nymphs of heaven passed that way, going to a festival on Mount Meru, they praised him. "Ask what you wish," he said. Some asked for the best of husbands, a lord among brahmans. "So be it," he said, and rose from the water. When the nymphs saw how crooked his body was, they laughed, and the sage cursed them: "You shall have the best of men for your husband, but because you laughed at my bent body, you shall afterward fall into the hands of thieves." They begged his pardon, and he softened: in time, he said, they would return to the world of the gods.

"It is because of that curse," Vyasa said, "that the wives of Krishna have now fallen into the hands of the barbarians. Do not grieve over it. All this destruction was worked by the lord of all — and your own end, too, is near, for he has drawn back your strength and your splendor. Death is the end of everyone born; a fall is the end of every rising; union ends in separation; growth tends to decay. Knowing this, the wise are touched by neither grief nor joy. Give everything up, go to the holy forest, and tell Yudhishthira that tomorrow, with his brothers, he must set out on the path of heroes."

Arjuna went back and told his brothers all that he had seen and heard. And the Pandavas placed Parikshit, the young heir of their house, on the throne, and went into the forest.
reflection: Vyasa's consolation rests on a single recognition: Krishna's coming and going alike were the working of time, which gives and takes away without partiality. The Ashtavakra story makes the point gently — even heavenly nymphs were promised to thieves by an old curse — so that Arjuna's defeat loses its sting: it was never his to keep, and never his loss alone.
tradition_note: The Bhagavata Purana gives a somewhat different account of Dwaraka's end and the deaths of the elders; this story follows the Vishnu Purana, as cited in the evidence pack.
content_note: Contains the funeral-pyre deaths of Krishna's queens and family elders after his death, and an attack by robbers; may warrant parental awareness for younger readers.
next_story_tease: The Pandavas turned their backs on the throne and took the road to the forest — and to Samanta-panchaka.
hero_scene: In a forest hermitage, the sage Vyasa raises a hand as he speaks to the dejected Arjuna, who lies prostrate before him with the great bow Gandiva lying slack beside him on the ground.
